b01.question: What is the punishment for compelling a person to render bonded labour?
b01.answer: Under section 16 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, any person who compels another to render bonded labour after the commencement of the Act is subject to a penalty of imprisonment for a term that may extend to three years. Additionally, the offender may be punished with a fine that may extend to two thousand rupees.

b02.question: Who bears the burden of proof when a debt is claimed to be a bonded debt?
b02.answer: Under section 15 of the Bonded Labour Act (1976), the burden of proof lies on the creditor to demonstrate that a debt is not a bonded debt whenever that debt is claimed to be a bonded debt by either a bonded labourer or a Vigilance Committee.

b03.question: What happened to bonded debts when the Act came into force?
b03.answer:
Upon the commencement of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, which is deemed to have come into force on October 25, 1975, the following actions occurred regarding bonded debts:

* **Extinguishment of Liability:** Every obligation of a bonded labourer to repay any bonded debt, or any portion of a debt that remained unsatisfied before the commencement of the Act, was deemed to be extinguished under section 6(1) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
* **Satisfaction of Decrees:** Any decree or order for the recovery of a bonded debt passed before the commencement of the Act that was not fully satisfied was deemed to be fully satisfied under section 6(3) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
* **Dismissal of Pending Proceedings:** Any pending suit or proceeding for the recovery of an advance made to a bonded labourer or for the enforcement of an obligation under the bonded labour system was dismissed under section 6(9) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
* **Prohibition of Recovery:** No suit or proceeding can be brought in any civil court or before any authority to recover any bonded debt under section 6(2) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
* **Vacation of Attachments:** Any attachment made before the commencement of the Act for the recovery of a bonded debt was vacated, and any movable property seized was required to be restored to the bonded labourer under section 6(4) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
* **Property Release:** Property belonging to a bonded labourer that was under mortgage, charge, or lien in connection with a bonded debt was freed and discharged from such encumbrances under section 7(1) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.

No suit or other proceeding lies in any civil court or before any other authority for the recovery of a bonded debt. b04.question: Can a freed bonded labourer be evicted from their homestead?
b04.answer: No, a freed bonded labourer cannot be evicted from their homestead or other residential premises that they occupied immediately before the commencement of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, if that occupancy was part of the consideration for their bonded labour. Under section 8 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, if such an eviction occurs after the commencement of the Act, the Executive Magistrate in charge of the Sub-Division where the premises are located is required to restore the labourer to possession of the property as early as practicable.

b06.question: What is the penalty if a creditor accepts payment against a debt that has already been extinguished?
b06.answer:
Under section 9 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, a creditor who accepts payment against a bonded debt that has been extinguished, deemed to be extinguished, or fully satisfied is subject to the following penalties:

*   **Imprisonment and Fine:** The creditor is punishable with imprisonment for a term that may extend to three years, in addition to a fine.
*   **Restitution:** The court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the creditor to deposit the amount accepted in contravention of the Act into the court. This amount is then to be refunded to the bonded labourer within a period specified by the court's order.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
There still exists in different parts of the country a system of usury under which the debtor or his 
descendants or dependants have to work for the creditor Without reasonable wages or with no wages in 
order to extinguish the debt. At times, several generations work under bond -age for the repayment of a 
paltry sum which had been taken by some remote ancestor. The interest rates are exorbitant and such 
bondage cannot be interpreted as the result of any legitimate contract or agreement. The system implies 
the infringement of the basic human rights and destruction of the dignity of human labour. 
2. Article 23(1) of the Constitution prohibits “beggar”, and other similar forms of forced labour and 
further provides that any contravention of the said prohibition shall be an offence punishable in 
accordance with law. Article 35(a) (ii) of the Constitution not only confers the power on Parliament to 
provide

accordance with law. Article 35(a) (ii) of the Constitution not only confers the power on Parliament to 
provide for punishment for the contravention of the said provisions of article 23(1) but expressly takes 
away the power of the State Legislature to make any legislation with regard to the said matter. 
Accordingly, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Ordinance, 1 975, was promulgated by the President 
on the 24th October, 1975. By the said Ordinance, the bonded labour system was abolished and the 
bonded labourers were freed and discharged from any obligation to render any bonded labour and their 
bonded debts were also extinguished. The Ordinance further affords protection to the freed bonded 
labourers from eviction from their homestead. Contraventions of the provisions of the Ordinance have 
been made offences punishable in accordance with law. Provisions for the foll ow-up measures and 
economic rehabilitation of the freed bonded labourers have also been made in the Ordinance.

w01.question: What is the overtime rate under the Code on Wages?
w01.answer: Under the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee who works in excess of the number of hours constituting a normal working day is entitled to be paid for every hour or part of an hour worked in excess at an overtime rate that is not less than twice the normal rate of wages.

bonus;  
(b) the provisions relating to wages shall be applicable to all employments covering both organised 
as well as un-organised sectors;

(d) it enables the appropriate Government to determine the factors by which the minimum wages

w05.question: What limits apply to fines imposed on an employee, and can a 14-year-old be fined?
w05.answer:
Under the Code on Wages (2019), there are several specific limits and conditions regarding the imposition of fines on employees:

*   **Age Restriction:** No fine may be imposed on any employee who is under the age of fifteen years; therefore, a 14-year-old cannot be fined under this Code.
*   **Monetary Limit:** The total amount of a fine imposed in any single wage-period cannot exceed three per cent of the wages payable to the employee for that specific period.
*   **Procedural Requirements:** Fines can only be imposed for acts or omissions previously specified by notice, and the employee must be given an opportunity to show cause against the fine. Furthermore, fines cannot be recovered in installments and must be imposed within ninety days of the act or omission. All fines must be recorded in a register, and the proceeds must be applied to purposes beneficial to the employees as approved by the prescribed authority.

w06.question: What is the minimum bonus payable under the Code on Wages?
w06.answer:
Under section 26(1) of the Code on Wages (2019), the annual minimum bonus payable to an eligible employee is calculated at the rate of eight and one-third per cent of the wages earned by the employee, or one hundred rupees, whichever is higher. This minimum bonus must be paid regardless of whether the employer had any allocable surplus during the previous accounting year, provided the employee has worked for at least thirty days in that accounting year. 

However, this amount is subject to the following conditions:

* Proportionate reduction: If an employee has not worked for all the working days in an accounting year, the minimum bonus may be proportionately reduced if the calculated amount is higher than eight and one-third per cent of the salary or wage for the days the employee actually worked (Section 27 of the Code on Wages (2019)).
* Deductions: Employers are entitled to deduct certain amounts from the bonus, such as previously paid puja or customary bonuses, interim bonus payments (Section 37 of the Code on Wages (2019)), or amounts corresponding to financial losses caused by an employee's misconduct (Section 38 of the Code on Wages (2019)).

4. The salient features of the Code on Wages, 2019, inter alia, are as follows:
(a) it provides for all essential elements relating to wages, equal remuneration, its payment and 
bonus;  
(b) the provisions relating to wages shall be applicable to all employments covering both organised 
as well as un-organised sectors; 
 (c) the power to fix minimum wages continues to be vested in the Central Government as well the 
State Government in their respective sphere;  
(d) it enables the appropriate Government to determine the factors by which the minimum wages 
shall be fixed for different category of employees. The factors shall be determined taking into account 
the skills required, the arduousness of the work assigned, geographical location of the workplace and 
other aspects which the appropriate Government considers necessary;

which are presently applicable only in respect of employees drawing wages of twenty -four thousand 
rupees per month, shall be made applicable to all employees irrespective of wage ceiling. The 
appropriate Government may extend the coverage of such provisions to the Government 
establishments also;

electronic mode or by crediting it in the bank account of the employee. However, the appropriate

39. Time limit for payment of bonus
(1) All amounts payable to an employee by way of bonus 
under this Code shall be paid by crediting it in the bank account of the employee by his employer within a 
period of eight months from the close of the accounting year: 
Provided that the appropriate Government or such authority as the appropriate Government may 
specify in this behalf may, upon an application made to it by the employer and for sufficient reasons, by 
order, extend the said period of eight months to such further period or periods as it thinks fit; so, however, 
that the total period so extended shall not in any case exceed two years. 
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub -section ( 1), where there is a dispute regarding 
payment of bonus pending before any authority, such bonus shall be paid, within a period of one month 
from the date on which the award becomes enforceable or the settlement comes into operation, in respect 
of such dispute: 
Provided that if, there is a dispute for payment at the higher rate, the employer shall pay eight and 
one-third per cent. of the wages earned by the employee as per the provisions of this Code within a period 
of eight months from the close of the accounting year.

w06.ground_truth: Under section 26(1) of the Code on Wages, 2019, an employee who has put in at least thirty days of work in an accounting year is entitled to an annual minimum bonus. The minimum bonus is eight and one-third per cent of the wages earned by the employee or one hundred rupees, whichever is higher. It is payable whether or not the employer has any allocable surplus.

w07.question: Within what time must bonus be paid?
w07.answer:
Under section 39 of the Code on Wages (2019), the general time limit for paying a bonus is within eight months from the close of the accounting year. This payment must be made by crediting the employee's bank account. The appropriate Government or a specified authority may extend this period for sufficient reasons, provided the total extension does not exceed two years.

There are specific exceptions to this general rule:

* If there is a dispute regarding the payment of a bonus pending before an authority, the bonus must be paid within one month from the date the award becomes enforceable or the settlement comes into operation.
* If the dispute concerns payment at a higher rate, the employer is still required to pay the minimum bonus of eight and one-third per cent of the wages earned by the employee within the standard eight-month period from the close of the accounting year.

w09.question: What is the time limit for filing a claim under the Code on Wages?
w09.answer: Under the Code on Wages, 2019, the period of limitation for a worker to file a claim is three years from the date on which the claim arises. This period was enhanced from the previous range of six months to two years to provide workers with more time to settle their claims. While the standard limit is three years, the authority appointed to hear the claim may entertain an application after this period if the applicant shows sufficient cause for the delay.

4. The salient features of the Code on Wages, 2019, inter alia, are as follows:
  
(q) it enables the appropriate Government to constitute Advisory Boards at Central and State level 
to advice the Central Government and the State Governments, respectively, on matters relating to 
wages, women employment, etc.;  
(r) the period of limitation for filing of claims by a worker has been enhanced to three years, as 
against the existing time period varying from six months to two years, to provide a worker more time 
to settle his claims.  
5. The Code on Wages, 2017, on similar lines, was introduced and referred to the Department -related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Labour, which submitted its forty -third Report on 18th December, 
2018. However, before the said Bill could be passed in the said House, it lapsed on dissolution of the 
Sixteenth Lok Sabha. Hence, the Code on Wages, 2019.

w10.question: What is the penalty for an employer who pays an employee less than the amount due, and what happens on a repeat offence?
w10.answer: Under section 54(1)(a) of the Code on Wages (2019), an employer who pays an employee less than the amount due is punishable with a fine that may extend to fifty thousand rupees. If the employer is convicted of a similar offence within five years of the first or subsequent offence, section 54(1)(b) stipulates that the penalty for the second or subsequent commission of the offence increases to imprisonment for a term that may extend to three months, a fine that may extend to one lakh rupees, or both.

w12.question: Is house rent allowance included in 'wages' under the Code on Wages?
w12.answer:
Under the Code on Wages (2019), house rent allowance is explicitly excluded from the definition of 'wages'. Section 2(y) of the Code on Wages (2019) defines 'wages' as all remuneration expressed in terms of money that would be payable if the terms of employment were fulfilled, but it provides a specific list of items that do not constitute wages, which includes 'house rent allowance' under clause (f). 

However, there is a specific provision regarding the computation of wages: the second proviso to section 2(y) states that for the purpose of equal wages to all genders and for the purpose of payment of wages, the emoluments specified in clause (f) (house rent allowance) shall be taken into account for the computation of wages.

w13.question: Can an offence under the Code on Wages be compounded, and at what cost?
w13.answer: Yes, offences under the Code on Wages, 2019, can be compounded, provided they are not punishable with imprisonment only or with both imprisonment and fine. Under section 56(1) of the Code on Wages, 2019, an accused person may apply to have an offence compounded either before or after the institution of a prosecution. The cost for compounding such an offence is set at fifty per cent. of the maximum fine provided for that specific offence.

w14.question: Who is excluded from the definition of 'worker' under the Code on Wages?
w14.answer:
Under the Code on Wages (2019), a person is excluded from the definition of 'worker' if they fall into any of the following categories:

* Individuals subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or the Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957).
* Individuals employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison.
* Individuals employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity.
* Individuals employed in a supervisory capacity who earn wages exceeding fifteen thousand rupees per month, or such other amount as may be notified by the Central Government from time to time.

o01.question: How many hours a day and days a week can a worker be required to work under the OSH Code?
o01.answer:
Under the OSH Code 2020, the working hours and days for a worker are regulated as follows:

*   **Daily Hours:** No worker may be required or allowed to work for more than eight hours in a day, as specified in section 25(1)(a) of the OSH Code 2020.
*   **Weekly Days:** No worker may be allowed to work in an establishment for more than six days in any one week, according to section 26(1) of the OSH Code 2020.

While these are the general limits, the OSH Code 2020 provides specific exceptions for motor transport undertakings. In such cases, an employer may require a worker to work on a scheduled weekly holiday to prevent service dislocation, provided that the worker does not work for more than ten days consecutively without a full day of rest intervening (section 26(1) of the OSH Code 2020).

o03.question: How much annual leave with wages is a worker entitled to under the OSH Code?
o03.answer:
Under the OSH Code (2020), a worker's entitlement to annual leave with wages is determined by the number of days they have worked in a calendar year, provided they have worked at least one hundred and eighty days. The specific rates of leave entitlement are as follows:

*   **General workers:** One day of leave for every twenty days of work.
*   **Adolescent workers:** One day of leave for every fifteen days of work.
*   **Workers employed below ground in a mine:** One day of leave for every fifteen days of work.

For workers whose service begins after the first day of January, they are entitled to leave at these same rates if they have worked for at least one-fourth of the total number of days remaining in that calendar year. Additionally, periods of layoff, maternity leave, or previously availed annual leave are counted toward the one hundred and eighty-day eligibility threshold, though workers do not earn leave for those specific counted periods. Holidays that fall between periods of leave are excluded from the calculation of leave taken.

o04.question: When must an employer appoint a safety officer?
o04.answer:
Under section 22(2) of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, an employer is required to appoint safety officers in the following types of establishments, provided they meet the specified worker thresholds:

*   Factories employing five hundred workers or more.
*   Factories carrying on a hazardous process employing two hundred fifty workers or more.
*   Building or other construction work sites employing two hundred fifty workers or more.
*   Mines employing one hundred workers or more.

The number of officers, their required qualifications, and their specific duties are to be prescribed by the appropriate Government.

o05.question: When is a canteen required, and when is a creche required?
o05.answer:
Under the OSH Code (2020), the requirements for canteens and crèches are as follows:

*   **Canteens:** An establishment is required to provide canteen facilities for its employees if it ordinarily employs one hundred or more workers, including contract labourers, as specified in section 24(1)(v) of the OSH Code (2020).
*   **Crèches:** The requirements for crèches depend on the type of establishment:
    *   **Plantations:** Employers must provide crèche facilities if fifty or more workers (including those employed by a contractor) are employed, or were employed on any day during the preceding twelve months, according to section 92(1)(b) of the OSH Code (2020).
    *   **General Establishments:** The Central Government may make rules requiring crèche facilities for children under the age of six years in establishments where more than fifty workers are ordinarily employed, as stated in section 24(3) of the OSH Code (2020).
    *   **Shared Premises:** Where premises are leased to different occupiers for use as separate factories, the owner and the occupiers are jointly and severally responsible for the provision and maintenance of common facilities, including crèches, as prescribed by the appropriate Government under section 80 of the OSH Code (2020).

In both plantation and general establishment settings, the code allows for flexibility: establishments may utilize common crèche facilities provided by the government, municipalities, private entities, or non-governmental organizations, or a group of establishments may pool their resources to set up a common crèche (section 92(1)(b) and section 24(3) of the OSH Code (2020)).

o06.question: Can women be employed at night under the OSH Code?
o06.answer: Yes, women can be employed at night under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. According to section 43 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, women are entitled to be employed in all establishments for all types of work and may be employed before 6 a.m. and beyond 7 p.m. with their consent. This employment is subject to conditions prescribed by the appropriate Government regarding safety, holidays, and working hours. This is further confirmed in section 13/14 of the same Code, which reiterates that women can work at night (beyond 7 PM and before 6 AM) provided there is consent and adherence to conditions relating to safety, holidays, and working hours.

o08.question: When do the contract labour provisions of the OSH Code apply?
o08.answer:
Under section 45 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, the provisions regarding contract labour apply to two specific categories of entities:

* Every establishment that employs, or has employed, fifty or more contract labour on any day during the preceding twelve months.
* Every manpower supply contractor who has employed fifty or more contract labour on any day during the preceding twelve months.

These provisions do not apply to establishments where the work performed is exclusively of an intermittent or casual nature. If a dispute arises regarding whether work is intermittent or casual, the appropriate Government makes the final decision after consulting with the National Board or a State Advisory Board. Work is not considered intermittent if it was performed for more than one hundred and twenty days in the preceding twelve months, or if it is of a seasonal character and performed for more than sixty days in a year.

o09.question: What happens if a contractor fails to pay wages to contract labour?
o09.answer:
Under section 55 of the OSH Code (2020), if a contractor fails to pay the full wages due to contract labour within the prescribed period, or makes a short payment, the following actions are taken:

* The principal employer becomes liable to pay the wages in full or the unpaid balance to the contract labour. The principal employer may then recover these payments from the contractor, either by deducting the amount from any funds payable to the contractor under a contract or by treating the amount as a debt payable by the contractor.
* The appropriate Government is required to issue orders to pay the outstanding wages using the security deposit that the contractor provided under their licence.

o10.question: When do the inter-State migrant worker provisions apply, and what travel benefit do such workers receive?
o10.answer:
The provisions regarding inter-State migrant workers apply to any establishment that employs ten or more inter-State migrant workers, or has employed that number on any day during the preceding twelve months, as stated in section 59 of the OSH Code 2020. 

Regarding travel benefits, section 61 of the OSH Code 2020 mandates that employers must pay a lump sum amount to every inter-State migrant worker to cover the fare for a to and fro journey between their place of employment and their native place once per year. The specific details regarding this payment—such as the minimum service required for entitlement, the periodicity, the class of travel, and other related matters—are to be determined by the appropriate Government.

o11.question: Which accidents must be notified under the OSH Code?
o11.answer:
Under section 10 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, an accident must be notified if it occurs at any place in an establishment and results in either:

*   The death of a person; or
*   Bodily injury that prevents the injured person from working for a period of forty-eight hours or more immediately following the accident; or
*   An accident of a nature prescribed by the appropriate Government.

Additionally, section 136 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, grants the Central Government the power to make regulations specifically for mines and dock work, which include the authority to specify the types of accidents that require notice under section 10.

o12.question: What is the general penalty for contravening the OSH Code?
o12.answer: Under section 94 of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (OSH Code 2020), the general penalty for contravening the provisions of the Code, or any rules, regulations, bye-laws, standards, or written orders made thereunder, applies to the employer or principal employer of an establishment. This penalty is set at a minimum of two lakh rupees and may extend up to three lakh rupees. Furthermore, if the contravention continues after a conviction, the employer is liable for an additional penalty that may extend to two thousand rupees for each day the contravention persists.

o14.question: What counts as a 'factory' and what counts as an 'establishment' under the OSH Code?
o14.answer:
Under the OSH Code (2020), the definitions for 'factory' and 'establishment' are as follows:

*   **Factory:** According to section 2(w), a factory is any premises (including its precincts) where a manufacturing process is carried on. It is defined by specific worker thresholds: 
    *   Twenty or more workers if the process uses power.
    *   Forty or more workers if the process does not use power.
    *   These thresholds apply to workers currently employed or those employed on any day of the preceding twelve months. Certain locations, such as mobile units of the armed forces, railway running sheds, hotels, restaurants, or eating places, are excluded. Additionally, if a State law in force prior to the Code specifies different worker thresholds, those State-specific numbers prevail until amended by the competent Legislature.
*   **Establishment:** According to section 2(v), an establishment is defined as:
    *   A place where any industry, trade, business, manufacturing, or occupation is carried on with ten or more workers.
    *   Specific entities such as motor transport undertakings, newspaper establishments, audio-video production, building and other construction work, or plantations, provided they employ ten or more workers.
    *   A factory (for the purposes of Chapter II) with ten or more workers, regardless of the worker threshold defined in clause (w).
    *   A mine, a port, or the vicinity of a port where dock work is carried out.
    *   The Code provides that the ten-worker threshold does not apply to establishments engaged in hazardous or life-threatening activities as notified by the Central Government.

o14.ground_truth: Under section 2(1)(w) of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (OSH Code), a factory is any premises on which twenty or more workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process is carried on with the aid of power. That threshold does not apply to an establishment carrying on a hazardous or life-threatening activity notified by the Central Government.

o15.question: What rights does an employee have when there is imminent danger at the workplace?
o15.answer:
When an employee has a reasonable apprehension of imminent serious personal injury, death, or danger to health at their workplace, they have the following rights and responsibilities under the OSH Code (2020):

* **Reporting:** The employee may bring the situation to the notice of their employer, either directly or through a member of the Safety Committee. Simultaneously, they must notify the Inspector-cum-Facilitator [1].
* **Remedial Action:** If the employer is satisfied that the imminent danger exists, they are required to take immediate remedial action and submit a report of that action to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator [1].
* **Dispute Resolution:** If the employer is not satisfied that the apprehended danger exists, they must refer the matter immediately to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator. The decision of the Inspector-cum-Facilitator regarding the existence of the imminent danger is final [2].

Additionally, for workers in factories engaged in hazardous processes, the OSH Code (2020) provides a specific right to warn about imminent danger to their lives or health. In these cases, workers may notify the occupier, agent, manager, or person in charge (directly or via the Safety Committee) and simultaneously notify the Inspector-cum-Facilitator. The person in charge must take immediate remedial action if satisfied, or otherwise refer the matter to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator for a final decision [3].

o16.question: Is employment of contract labour allowed in an establishment's core activity?
o16.answer:
Under section 57 of the OSH Code (2020), the employment of contract labour in the core activities of an establishment is generally prohibited. However, a principal employer may engage contract labour for a core activity through a contractor if any of the following conditions are met:

* The normal functioning of the establishment is such that the activity is ordinarily done through a contractor.
* The activities do not require full-time workers for the major portion of the working hours in a day or for longer periods.
* There is a sudden increase in the volume of work in the core activity that must be accomplished within a specified time.

For the purposes of this code, a "core activity" is defined in section 2(p) of the OSH Code (2020) as any activity for which the establishment is set up, including any activity essential or necessary to that purpose. The section also provides a list of specific activities—such as sanitation, security, canteen services, and loading/unloading—that are not considered essential or necessary if the establishment was not specifically set up for them.

x01.question: How does the Bonded Labour Act define 'nominal wages', and how does that relate to minimum wages legislation?
x01.answer:
Under section 2(i) of the Bonded Labour Act (1976), "nominal wages" are defined as wages that are less than the minimum wages fixed by the Government for the same or similar labour under any law currently in force. In instances where no such minimum wage has been established for a specific form of labour, nominal wages are defined as those that are less than the wages normally paid to labourers performing the same or similar work in the same locality.

This definition directly links the concept of nominal wages to the broader framework of minimum wage legislation by using the government-mandated minimum rate as the benchmark for identifying underpayment. The Bonded Labour Act (1976) identifies the payment of nominal wages (or the absence of wages) as a key characteristic of the "bonded labour system," which involves forced or partly forced labour performed under various debt-related or social obligations, as outlined in section 2(g) of the Bonded Labour Act (1976).

x02.question: Does the definition of 'contract labour' differ between the Code on Wages and the OSH Code?
x02.answer:
The definition of 'contract labour' is identical in both the Code on Wages (2019) and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020). Under section 2(g) of the Code on Wages (2019) and section 2(m) of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020), 'contract labour' is defined as a worker hired in or in connection with the work of an establishment by or through a contractor, regardless of whether the principal employer has knowledge of the hiring. Both definitions explicitly include inter-State migrant workers.

Furthermore, both codes provide the same exclusion: the term does not include a worker (other than a part-time employee) who meets both of the following criteria:

* The worker is regularly employed by the contractor for any activity of the contractor's establishment, and their employment is governed by mutually accepted standards of conditions of employment, including engagement on a permanent basis.
* The worker receives periodical increments in pay, social security coverage, and other welfare benefits in accordance with the law in force for that employment.

Under section 2(g) of the Code on Wages, 2019, contract labour means a worker deemed to be employed in or in connection with the work of an establishment when hired in or in connection with such work by or through a contractor, with or without the knowledge of the principal employer. x03.question: Both the Code on Wages and the OSH Code provide for overtime. Do they set the same rate?
x03.answer: Yes, both the Code on Wages (2019) and the OSH Code (2020) set the same rate for overtime work. Under section 14 of the Code on Wages (2019), an employer is required to pay for overtime work at a rate not less than twice the normal rate of wages. Similarly, section 27 of the OSH Code (2020) stipulates that wages for overtime work shall be paid at the rate of twice the rate of wages.

x04.question: Does the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act cover contract labour and inter-State migrant workers?
x04.answer: Yes, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, covers contract labour and inter-State migrant workers. According to the explanation provided under section 2(g) of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, it is declared for the removal of doubts that any system of forced or partly forced labour is included under the definition of a "bonded labour system" if it requires a workman who is defined as contract labour under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, or an inter-State migrant workman as defined under the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, to render labour or service under the circumstances or disabilities specified in the Act.

x05.question: Both Codes make company officers liable for offences. What must be proved against a director?
x05.answer:
Under both the Code on Wages (2019) and the OSH Code (2020), a director, manager, secretary, or other officer of a company can be held liable for an offence committed by the company if it is proven that the offence was committed with their consent or connivance, or if the offence is attributable to any neglect on their part. 

Specifically:
* Under section 55 of the Code on Wages (2019), if an offence is committed by a company, any director, manager, secretary, or other officer is deemed guilty if the offence was committed with their consent or connivance, or is attributable to their neglect.
* Under section 109 of the OSH Code (2020), the same standard applies: a director, manager, company secretary, or other officer is deemed guilty if the offence was committed with their consent or connivance, or is attributable to their neglect.
